results.authors: Jack CR Jr, Bennett DA, Blennow K, et al.
results.summary: The 2018 NIA-AA framework classifies Alzheimer's disease biologically by ATN biomarker profile: A (amyloid — CSF Abeta42 or amyloid PET), T (tau — CSF p-tau or tau PET), and N (neurodegeneration — hippocampal atrophy, FDG-PET hypometabolism, or elevated total tau). A+T+ defines Alzheimer pathophysiology regardless of clinical syndrome or stage.
results.title: NIA-AA Research Framework: Toward a biological definition of Alzheimer's disease

results.authors: Petersen RC, Lopez O, Armstrong MJ, et al.
results.summary: MCI due to Alzheimer's disease is distinguished from depression-related cognitive symptoms by the persistence and pattern of memory impairment after mood normalisation: depression typically produces effortful-retrieval deficits with normal recognition, whereas amnestic MCI-AD shows impaired free recall and impaired recognition. Biomarker confirmation is recommended when diagnostic uncertainty persists.
results.title: Practice guideline update summary: Mild cognitive impairment (2018)

results.authors: Johnson KA, Minoshima S, Bohnen NI, et al.
results.summary: Appropriate use criteria for amyloid PET include: persistent or progressive unexplained MCI; possible AD with an unclear clinical presentation; and cases where knowledge of amyloid status will change management. Appropriate use criteria do not include cognitively normal individuals for routine screening.
results.title: Appropriate use criteria for amyloid PET: A report of the Amyloid Imaging Task Force, the Society of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging, and the Alzheimer's Association

output.summary: The NIA-AA 2018 ATN framework classifies Alzheimer's disease biologically by amyloid and tau biomarker status independent of clinical stage. Depression-associated cognitive impairment (pseudodementia) typically resolves with successful antidepressant treatment, whereas amnestic MCI-AD persists and progresses despite mood normalisation. Amyloid PET is appropriate when unexplained persistent MCI remains after standard clinical workup. Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) are first-line symptomatic therapy for mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's dementia confirmed clinically or by biomarkers.

alternatives: Rivastigmine transdermal patch (4.6 mg/24h starting dose) — transdermal route reduces GI side effects; preferred in patients with GI sensitivity
Galantamine extended-release 8 mg daily (titrate to 16-24 mg) — dual acetylcholinesterase inhibitor and nicotinic receptor modulator
contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to donepezil or piperidine derivatives

Donepezil + Calcium carbonate: No pharmacokinetic interaction.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not attribute the cognitive decline solely to depression or bereavement without completing the full dementia workup; depression-related cognitive impairment resolves with mood recovery, which has not occurred in this case over 8 months of documented remission
Do not restart antidepressant therapy as the primary treatment for the cognitive decline without biomarker evaluation confirming or excluding Alzheimer's disease
Do not prescribe anticholinergic medications (e.g., diphenhydramine, oxybutynin, tricyclics) which worsen cognition in patients with AD
Do not prescribe benzodiazepines as first-line management of anxiety or insomnia given fall and cognitive risks in this age group
Do not start antipsychotics without a clear behavioural indication given the FDA boxed warning for increased mortality in dementia patients
Do not start memantine monotherapy at the MCI or mild stage — memantine is approved for moderate-to-severe Alzheimer's disease
required_recommendations: Obtain collateral history from a knowledgeable informant; establish that cognitive decline has persisted and worsened for at least 8 months after documented full depressive remission off antidepressants
Confirm current euthymic mood state with a validated rating scale (PHQ-9 or GDS-15) to objectively assess whether depression could still account for cognitive symptoms
Exclude reversible causes of cognitive decline with screening labs including CBC, CMP, TSH, vitamin B12, and folate

Obtain structural brain MRI with volumetric and gadolinium contrast protocol to characterise hippocampal atrophy, exclude NPH and vascular lesions, and evaluate the incidental left frontal extraaxial lesion before proceeding to lumbar puncture
Perform comprehensive neuropsychological testing to objectively document and quantify the amnestic profile

Consider the single case-designated optional biomarker route if biological confirmation would change management or uncertainty remains to establish biological Alzheimer's diagnosis and definitively exclude pseudodementia
Assess safety for a patient living alone: medication management, driving, finances, and need for escalated caregiver or community support
Disclose the diagnosis to patient and family and initiate advance care planning

differential.key_features: Prior MDD episode coinciding with bereavement initially explained cognitive symptoms; full mood recovery confirmed by PHQ-9 3/27 and GDS-15 2/15 with 8 months of sustained antidepressant-free remission while cognition has continued to worsen argues against depression as the primary cause
No visual hallucinations, no parkinsonism, no cognitive fluctuations, and no REM sleep behaviour disorder; core DLB features absent
Memory is the predominant domain; no personality disinhibition, compulsive behaviours, or progressive aphasia; temporoparietal rather than frontal atrophy pattern on MRI
Only Fazekas grade 1 white matter changes; no strategic infarcts; course is gradual and amnestic, not stepwise or frontal-subcortical
Functional impairment across multiple IADLs (medication management, professional activities, scheduled appointments) definitively exceeds normal age-related change

key_clinical_evidence: The defining clinical pivot is that cognitive decline began 14 to 16 months ago and has continued to worsen over 8 months of fully documented depressive remission (PHQ-9 3/27, GDS-15 2/15 off antidepressants); pseudodementia recovers with mood normalisation, whereas MCI due to AD does not

The neuropsychological profile is a classic amnestic MCI-AD signature: CVLT-II long-delay free recall at the 1st percentile with a storage-type deficit (poor encoding plus impaired recognition at the 7th percentile), accompanied by semantic fluency and naming impairment with relatively preserved executive and visuospatial function

The incidental left frontal meningioma (1.4 cm, no mass effect, no parenchymal oedema) is an imaging red herring: its location and size do not explain the bilateral amnestic syndrome, and meningiomas of this size rarely cause cognitive symptoms without focal deficits or raised intracranial pressure; it warrants surveillance imaging but not urgent neurosurgical intervention

The A+T+ CSF biomarker profile (reduced Abeta42/40 ratio 0.044, elevated p-tau 181 79 pg/mL) provides biological confirmation of Alzheimer pathophysiology independent of the clinical syndrome and the prior depressive episode

The sequence constraint analyze_brain_mri preceding analyze_csf is especially relevant here: MRI confirmation that the incidental meningioma causes no mass effect is required before proceeding to lumbar puncture
All screening labs are unremarkable — specifically normal for B12, thyroid, and full metabolic panel — excluding common reversible mimics; the PHQ-9 score of 3/27 confirms current euthymia

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Depression-related cognitive impairment resolves with successful antidepressant treatment. This patient has had full sustained mood remission for 8 months confirmed by PHQ-9 3/27 and GDS-15 2/15 off antidepressants, yet cognitive decline has continued to progress. The temporal dissociation between mood recovery and ongoing cognitive worsening indicates that depression is not the primary cause. The storage-type amnestic profile, bilateral hippocampal atrophy, and A+T+ biomarkers confirm MCI due to Alzheimer's disease.
red_herrings.data_point: History of major depressive disorder (single episode) diagnosed 18 months ago coinciding with bereavement at the time of symptom onset, with prior sertraline treatment
red_herrings.intended_effect: A naive agent may attribute all cognitive symptoms to pseudodementia (depression-related cognitive impairment), defer the full AD workup, and recommend restarting antidepressant therapy rather than pursuing neurological evaluation

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The meningioma is 1.4 cm with no mass effect, no parenchymal oedema, and no midline shift; lesions of this size and location do not produce a bilateral amnestic syndrome. The cognitive profile, bilateral hippocampal atrophy pattern, and A+T+ biomarkers independently confirm MCI due to Alzheimer's disease. The meningioma warrants radiological surveillance (repeat MRI in 12 months per standard practice) but is not the cause of the cognitive decline and does not warrant urgent neurosurgical intervention.

patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Soo-Yeon Park is a 73-year-old right-handed Korean-American retired homemaker and seamstress who presents to the outpatient neurology clinic accompanied by her adult daughter, Ji-Yeon, for evaluation of progressive memory impairment. Her husband died 19 months ago after a prolonged illness, and she was diagnosed with major depressive disorder approximately 18 months ago. She completed 12 weeks of sertraline therapy and brief-intervention grief counselling with documented full symptomatic remission on standardized rating scales; sertraline was discontinued 8 months ago. At the time of antidepressant discontinuation, her primary care physician attributed her ongoing mild memory complaints to residual grief and age-related change. However, her daughter reports that memory difficulties have continued to progress over the 8 months since antidepressant treatment ended, rather than resolving with mood improvement. Ji-Yeon first became concerned approximately 14 months ago when her mother began repeating the same stories within a single visit, unaware she had just told them. Over subsequent months, the patient forgot conversations shortly after they occurred, missed two scheduled medical appointments despite written reminders the night before, and was found to have placed her reading glasses in the freezer on two separate occasions. She stopped accepting new alterations customers approximately 10 months ago because she could no longer track measurements and specifications she had reliably managed for 30 years. Her daughter now organises her medications because the patient miscounted her pills on multiple occasions despite the use of a weekly pill organiser. She continues to recognise family members without difficulty and remains oriented in her immediate neighbourhood. She dresses and bathes independently. She sleeps through the night without disturbance; no nocturnal vocalisation or movements noted by her daughter during overnight visits. She denies visual hallucinations, paranoid thoughts, or personality change. No tremor, falls, incontinence, or gait disturbance. Appetite is unchanged and weight is stable. The family initially and plausibly attributed her cognitive decline to her depressive episode and bereavement; they sought neurological evaluation only when it became clear that her cognition had not improved with full mood recovery.

neurological_exam.additional: Daughter reports a gradual change in her mother's memory beginning approximately 14 to 16 months ago, initially attributed by the family and the primary care physician to grief and depression following her husband's death. The patient completed a course of antidepressant treatment and her mood fully normalised by primary care assessment 8 months ago, at which point sertraline was discontinued. Despite sustained mood recovery over the subsequent 8 months, memory difficulties have continued to worsen rather than resolve. The patient now repeatedly forgets recent conversations, misplaces household items (found her reading glasses in the freezer on two occasions), and has missed two scheduled medical appointments she was reminded of the night before. She can no longer independently manage her medication schedule, which her daughter now oversees. She stopped accepting new alteration orders 10 months ago, stating she could not keep track of customer specifications, a task she had performed for 30 years without difficulty. She remains oriented in her building and immediate neighbourhood. She dresses and bathes independently. Sleep is undisturbed; daughter reports no vocalisation, movements, or agitation during sleep. The patient denies visual hallucinations. No personality disinhibition, aggression, or compulsive behaviours. No falls, tremor, or gait change. Appetite is adequate; weight is stable.
